newsitem.title: GERMANY: Key European copper group wants speedy LME reform.
newsitem.headline: Key European copper group wants speedy LME reform.

text.p: Copper and copper alloy specialist KM Europa Metal Group (KME) is pressing for more transparency on the London Metal Exchange (LME), board spokesman Norbert Brodersen said.
"We need increased transparency in every respect and the strategy chosen points in the right direction," he said in an interview with Reuters after a company results briefing.
"But change is happening more slowly than anticipated and the question is should it not be enacted faster, seeing the backwardation that is currently building up," he asked.
"Structures need to be discussed and changed to ensure that the regulatory instruments in place are sufficient to keep artificial volatility in check."
"One area would be the possible separation of options trade from the LME, similar to the practice in the United States."
LME Chief Executive David King last week said reforms in response to the Sumitomo Corp affair last year, would largely be in place by the end of 1997.
Brodersen said volatility was not a problem for KME, which considers LME trading a neutral factor in its own financial results and which does not speculate on LME prices.
But customers buying its semi-finished products, some 720,000 tonnes of sheet, bars, tubes and cables in 1996, were more exposed to damaging copper price fluctuations.
They were eagerly awaiting measures to avoid another Sumitomo-style debacle in which copper prices collapsed last year as a result of illegitimate speculative activity.
KME was actively and directly involved in discussions with the UK Securities and Investment Board (SIB) and the LME board and chairman on how to implement necessary changes.
The daily reporting of LME warehouse stocks was one positive step but the make-up of the LME board needed to be improved and the LME should also adress conflicts of interest.
The role of the LME chief executive and his executive staff needed to be strenghtened and allow for quick interventio.
Brodersen also said LME crises of recent years had emphasised the need for competition in the form of an enhanced role for the New York (COMEX) copper contract in Europe.
"Why is the Commodity Exchange not more involved over here in establishing prices and arbitrage facilities," he asked.
"Why is it establishing a new warehouse in Chile, where there is no consumption, but not over here?"
The influence of fundamentals and the role of institutional investors on the LME had changed dramatically since the late 1980s, Brodersen said.
This had moved LME turnover to 50 to 100 times the world's annual consumption of copper and the LME price had become mostly the result of non-demand factors.
KME believed supply fundamentals looked comfortable for 1997 and 1998 despite interruptions to mine output in some African countries, and this should weigh on prices.
The flow of former Soviet Union material should also continue unabated. Consumption was not rising as fast.

But the current backwardation belied the fact physical copper was widely available in Europe. Grade A was relatively tighter as Far Eastern prices were better but standard grades and scrap were abundant.
KME, the result of an amalgamation of companies across Europe two years ago, operates 18 plants in four countries and accounts for 70 percent of European copper semis production.
It is part of the Italian SMI - Soc Metallurgica Italiana SpA group.
